There are two ways to find cell types in cytometry data, and they make opposite
mistakes.

cyRAVEN takes rules you wrote and applies them, then checks whether the rules
held. cyCONDOR groups cells by similarity and works out afterwards what each group
was.

For many projects the sensible thing is to run both, because each one is blind to
its own kind of error.

**Rules can only find what you thought of.** If your blood samples contain a cell
population nobody has written a definition for, no amount of careful gating will
reveal it. There is no rule for it to break.

**Grouping cannot tell you a rule is wrong.** It will always return groups,
whatever you give it, and it has no expectation to contradict. It also involves
its own judgement calls, made after seeing the data: how many groups to ask for,
which proteins to use, how to scale them. That moves the subjectivity somewhere
else rather than removing it.

Run both and each is checked by something that does not share its assumptions.
This is established practice, not a novelty. The DAFi method was built on exactly
this idea, using a gating strategy to steer the clustering, and it recovers rare
populations that neither approach finds cleanly alone
([Lee et al., 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29665244/)).

## The division of labour

| You want to know | Use | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Does population X differ between groups | cyRAVEN | Populations are defined in advance and tested with donors as replicates |
| Are my gates in the right place | cyRAVEN | Threshold drift, the phenotype heatmap and the gate against cluster check all exist to say no |
| Is there something here I did not name | Both | cyRAVEN flags the undescribed cluster, cyCONDOR characterises it properly |
| What is that cluster, in gateable terms | cyRAVEN | `--explain-clusters` turns it into two-marker gates with held-out metrics |
| Is there a developmental trajectory | cyCONDOR | Diffusion maps and Slingshot, which cyRAVEN does not have |
| Can I transfer labels to a new cohort | cyCONDOR | Trained classifiers and label transfer |
| I have FlowJo gates already | cyCONDOR | It reads `.wsp` workspaces, cyRAVEN only writes FCS out |
| How many clusters are really there | cyCONDOR | Phenograph picks its own count instead of taking it as a setting |
| Can I correct this batch effect safely | cyRAVEN | It measures the batch and group overlap first and refuses when correction would delete the finding |

## Three questions, and how to answer them with both

### "My CD4 T cell frequency dropped in the patient group. Is that real?"

This is the question cyRAVEN was built for, and the trap is that a frequency can
fall for reasons that have nothing to do with CD4 T cells.

Run cyRAVEN with `--cluster`. Then read four things in order.

`threshold_drift_stats.csv` first. If CD4 is flagged, the per-sample cuts moved
systematically between your groups, and part of the drop is a change in the
definition. Stop here and look at the densities.

`compositional_concordance.csv` second. Percentages are forced to sum to 100, so
if another population expanded, CD4 falls without losing a single cell. A finding
that is significant on raw percentages but not on centred log-ratios is telling
you exactly that.

`cluster_gate_agreement_populations.csv` third. If CD4 T cells are scattered
across several clusters, the label is covering more than one phenotype and the
overall frequency is an average of things that may be moving in different
directions.

`confounding_diagnostics.csv` last, for whether age or sex differs between your
groups and tracks the outcome.

cyCONDOR is not needed for this one. Bring it in only if step three showed the
label covering several phenotypes, in which case you want to know what they are.

### "There is a cluster nobody expected. What is it, and does it matter?"

This needs both tools and a specific order.

Start with cyRAVEN and `--cluster --explain-clusters`. The gate against cluster
table tells you a cluster is dominated by the catch-all label, which is the
signal that your specification does not describe it.
`cluster_gate_proposals.csv` then gives you a short sequence of two-marker gates
that select those cells, with performance measured on held-out cells. That is
already enough to go back to the cytometer and draw it.

Now move to cyCONDOR for characterisation. Its per-marker plots
(`plot_marker_ridgeplot`, `plot_marker_violinplot`, `plot_marker_dotplot`) show
the full intensity distribution of that population rather than a single median,
and `plot_marker_group_HM` compares it across your groups. If the cells look like
they might sit on a differentiation axis, `runDM` and `runPseudotime` will tell
you whether there is a trajectory through them.

Finally, come back to cyRAVEN. Add the population to your `populations:` block
using the markers the proposal named, rerun, and it is now a named population
with a per-sample frequency and a proper test. The discovery was
data-driven, the definition is written down, and the test is done on donors.

That last step matters. A population found by clustering and tested by clustering
on the same cells has been chosen because it was separable in these samples. Once
it is a written gate, the next cohort tests it honestly.

### "I need this to hold up across sites, or across three years of acquisition."

The obstacle here is people, not reagents. Expert operators gating the same files
report population sizes that differ by around a third, and once more than one
person is analysing, that human variation accounts for the majority of the
technical noise in the study
([Cadwell et al., 2021](http://journal.pda.org/content/75/1/33)). Standardising
the antibodies alone does not fix it. EuroFlow only got between-centre variation
below 7% once they standardised the analysis as well
([Kalina et al., 2012](https://www.nature.com/articles/leu2012122)).

Use cyRAVEN as the primary analysis, because writing the definitions down and
placing each cut-off from the data takes the operator out of the step where that
variation enters. Keep the config file in version control next to the results,
and keep `run_manifest.txt`, which records the software versions and the exact
code used.

Use cyCONDOR periodically as an independent audit. Cluster the accumulated data
without reference to the specification and check that the populations you have
been reporting still come back as coherent clusters. If a population starts
splitting or merging, something changed in acquisition and the specification
needs revisiting.

## Running both on one dataset

The two tools read the same FCS files. cyCONDOR wants an annotation table whose
first column names the files, which is the same information a cyRAVEN sample map
carries, so one file can be rewritten for the other rather than maintained twice.

```r
# cyRAVEN
run_cyraven(list(
  dir = "data/fcs/", outdir = "results_cyraven/",
  sample_map = "data/sample_map.csv",
  config = "data/my_panel.yaml",
  group_column = "cohort", reference_group = "Healthy controls",
  unsupervised = TRUE, explain_clusters = TRUE
))

# cyCONDOR, same files
anno <- read.csv("data/sample_map.csv")
write.csv(anno, "results_condor/anno_table.csv", row.names = FALSE)

condor <- cyCONDOR::prep_fcd(
  data_path = "data/fcs/", max_cell = 30000, useCSV = FALSE,
  transformation = "auto_logi", remove_param = c("Time", "InFile"),
  anno_table = "results_condor/anno_table.csv",
  filename_col = "file", seed = 42)
condor <- cyCONDOR::runPCA(condor, data_slot = "orig", seed = 42)
condor <- cyCONDOR::runUMAP(condor, input_type = "pca", data_slot = "orig", seed = 42)
condor <- cyCONDOR::runFlowSOM(condor, input_type = "pca", data_slot = "orig",
                               nClusters = 8, seed = 42)
```

The `benchmark/` directory in the cyRAVEN repository runs both on a small public
dataset and writes the comparison, if you want a worked example to copy.

## Do not expect the pictures to match

The two UMAPs will look nothing alike, and that is not a bug in either tool. On
the benchmark dataset the difference comes from four things, in order of size:

cyCONDOR embeds every event in the files. cyRAVEN embeds only cells that passed
scatter, singlet, viability and CD45 gating. Part of the cyCONDOR map is debris.

cyCONDOR includes the scatter channels in its feature set. Scatter spans decades
and carries far more variance than any fluorescence marker, so it dominates the
principal components the embedding is built on. Much of the structure in that map
is cell size and granularity. cyRAVEN uses scatter to gate and then drops it.

cyCONDOR embeds principal component scores, cyRAVEN embeds the marker matrix
directly, which changes which cells are neighbours before the graph is built.

The two use different transforms by default, so the same raw intensity sits in a
different place on each axis.

Comparing the two pictures directly is the mistake. Compare the tables.

## How many groups is the right number?

There is no right number, and this is worth being clear-eyed about.

On the benchmark data, FlowSOM asked for 8 groups returns 8. Phenograph, which
decides for itself, returns 24 on exactly the same cells. Both are reasonable
algorithms behaving correctly. Neither number is the number of cell populations
that exist in blood.

The practical consequence: if a finding appears at 8 groups and disappears at 24,
it is a finding about the setting rather than about the biology. Check that it
survives a different choice before you believe it.

If you want a default, FlowSOM is a safe one. It performed at or near the top
across every dataset in the standard comparison of clustering methods, and it is
fast enough to be a routine cross-check rather than an afternoon's work
([Weber and Robinson, 2016](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/cyto.a.23030)).

## Further reading

- [Lee et al., 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29665244/), the DAFi method,
  which uses a gating strategy to steer clustering.
- [Briefings in Bioinformatics, 2025](https://academic.oup.com/bib/article/26/1/bbae633/7916377),
  a systematic comparison of manual gating, clustering and automated gating
  across 23 tools.
- [Weber and Robinson, 2016](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/cyto.a.23030),
  the benchmark that made FlowSOM the default choice.
- [Kalina et al., 2012](https://www.nature.com/articles/leu2012122), how EuroFlow
  achieved comparable results across centres.
- [Cadwell et al., 2021](http://journal.pda.org/content/75/1/33), how much
  variation between operators actually contributes.
